description: Somos COSMIC TRACE, un equipo que busca unir la ciencia, tecnología y la exploración espacial. Buscamos acercar a los jóvenes al legado de las misiones de la NASA mediante una solución innovadora que transformará los datos científicos en historia que merecen ser contadas.
summary:
Cosmic Trace is an interactive educational platform that seeks to uncover the stories behind the artifacts humanity has left in space since the 1960s. Through a map of the solar system, digital dossiers, actual photographs, timelines, and interactive challenges, users can explore space missions and discover the fate of the technological craft involved.

Our project addresses this challenge by transforming scientific information into engaging, accessible stories tailored for a younger audience. Each dossier includes details such as the artifact’s current status, its location, its original mission, its scientific discoveries, interesting trivia, and the unique characteristics that set it apart. Furthermore, we incorporate visual resources and interactive 3D models to bring these objects closer to the user.

Cosmic Trace is significant because it fosters an appreciation for scientific progress, helps us understand the legacy of space exploration, and encourages reflection on the footprint we leave on other worlds. After all, while some missions may come to an end, their stories endure.
details:
COSMIC TRACE: Lost but Not Forgotten Objects

Educational Platform and Statistical Analysis of Space Missions

Gabriel Briceño, Alejandra Altamiza, Andrea Benavides, Karla Mariñas and Frank Poma

Team from Lima, Peru

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

November 15, 2026

 

Summary

COSMIC TRACE is an educational and science outreach resource that brings together sixteen objects that humanity left on the Moon, Mars, and in deep space, from the Surveyor 3 probe (1967) to the Ingenuity rover (2021). The project combines an interactive timeline, 360° exploration, fourteen 3D models, a statistical analysis of mission durations, and an interactive simulator. Its purpose is to help anyone understand what we left in space, how long it functioned, and what factors influence whether a space mission succeeds or fails.

Problem and Motivation

Every space voyage leaves tangible traces: inactive probes, landers, scientific instruments, and rovers that have reached the end of their lifespan. However, this history is often scattered across technical files that are difficult for the general public to access, and the question of how long these spacecraft actually operate is rarely answered.

Our starting point was a simple question: what was left behind in space and how long did each mission last? We believe that scientific curiosity stems from asking clear questions, so we transformed official NASA records into a visual, understandable, and interactive experience for young people and students.

Goals

General Objective

To clearly and attractively disseminate the history, location, and operational duration of objects that humanity left on the Moon, Mars, and deep space, based on open data from NASA.

Specific Objectives

·    Chronological organization: Present sixteen historical objects between 1967 and 2021, each with its information sheet.

·    Visual space exploration: Allows its location and tour using the official NASA Eyes viewer and interactive 3D models.

·    Duration analysis: Compare how long the missions sent to the Moon and Mars were able to operate.

·    Educational simulation: Offer a ship designer that estimates duration, cost, and travel time based on design decisions.

·    Reinforcement of learning: Consolidate the knowledge acquired through an interactive questionnaire and official sources.

Solution Development

The web platform guides the user progressively from historical exploration to statistical analysis and interactive experimentation.

Timeline, 360° Explorer and 3D Lab

On the timeline, each of the sixteen objects appears in the year it arrived at its destination (1967–2021) with a summary document that illustrates the intense space race of the 1960s and 70s, the lunar hiatus of the 1980s, and the current return to space exploration. The 360° Explorer integrates the official NASA Eyes viewer (with a direct alternate link), while the 3D Lab brings together fourteen rotating models—such as the Surveyor probes, the Eagle lunar module, and its retroreflector—to appreciate their true scale.

Survival Analysis: Moon vs. Mars

To answer how long spacecraft remain operational after reaching their destination, 108 operational missions from NASA's NSSDCA archive were analyzed (71 operational lunar missions after excluding intentional impact stages and 37 Martian missions; NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive [NSSDCA], 2024a, 2024b). As summarized in Table 1, missions to Mars have a longer duration than lunar missions.

The difference between the median (85 days) and the average (1,929 days) on Mars has a clear explanation: several missions fail at the beginning of their journey or during arrival, but those that manage to survive operate for years—some for over 25 years—significantly raising the average. Therefore, looking only at the average without the median can give a misleading picture. This section is accompanied by a stepwise survival curve and a graph by decade from the 1950s to the 2020s.

Interactive Lab “Design Your Spaceship”, Questionnaire and Sources

In the interactive simulator, the user configures a mission by choosing its destination (the Moon, with a travel time of approximately 3.6 days, or Mars, with a travel time of approximately 180 days), its architecture (orbiter, lander, or rover), its weight (between 50 and 8,500 kg), and its launch decade (1960 to 2020). With this data, the tool instantly calculates the expected duration, the estimated cost in millions of dollars, the travel time, and the mission profile. It also includes buttons to load real missions such as Perseverance, Chandrayaan-3, and Hope, or future projects like Chang'e 7, MMX, ESCAPADE, and Rosalind Franklin. Finally, an interactive quiz reinforces learning, and a list of official sources encourages further research.

Methodology

Data Sources and Cleaning

A total of 133 official records were compiled from NASA portals: 96 objects on the Moon (49 photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, 29 with approximate locations, and 18 missing and unlocated; NSSDCA, 2024a) and 37 missions to Mars (28 successful or active and 9 unsuccessful; NSSDCA, 2024b). To study the actual lifespan of operational spacecraft, the database was cleaned by removing 24 pieces manufactured to be intentionally crashed (such as rocket stages and impactors) and one record with no confirmed weight, leaving 108 operational missions. Furthermore, the histories of the 11 spacecraft still operating today (3 on the Moon and 8 on Mars) were not closed: the number of days they have been active up to November 15, 2026, was simply counted (data redacted).

Survival Analysis

Using the Kaplan-Meier method, the number of spacecraft still active day after day was calculated, yielding the typical (median) lifespan, the actual average lifespan, and the percentage of active spacecraft after 1 and 8 years. The Log-Rank test confirmed that the longer lifespan observed on Mars compared to the Moon is not due to chance. Then, using a stratified Cox model, it was assessed whether weight or landing shortened the lifespan by comparing each spacecraft only with others from the same destination and era, preventing older technology from distorting the modern one. Finally, different accelerated time models (AFT) were compared, and the Weibull model was selected, as it best explained the actual lifespans and allowed for verification that every ten years, spacecraft last almost twice as long (1.89 times longer).

Models from the "Design Your Ship" Simulator

The simulator translates the user's four decisions (destination, ship type, weight, and decade) into realistic estimates supported by three statistical techniques:

·    Expected duration (AFT Weibull model): Apply the adjusted equation to the 108 operational missions to estimate how many typical days (median) the ship would be able to work after arriving at its destination.

·    Estimated cost (GLM Gamma with logarithmic link): Adjusted over the 43 missions with reported public budget, it starts from a historical base and multiplies the cost if the destination is Mars (2.20 times more) or if the spacecraft lands (1.78 times more), gradually adjusting it according to weight and decade.

·    Travel time and mission profile (PCA and K-Means): Summarizes the patterns found when classifying the 126 missions with complete data into three actual profiles: long-duration explorers, early failures, and large, fast lunar spacecraft.

Web Development

The platform was built as a static, open website in HTML, Tailwind CSS, and JavaScript, integrating Chart.js for interactive visualizations, dynamic vector graphics (SVG) for spacecraft architectures, 3D models with Three.js, and the NASA Eyes viewer.

Results, Limitations and Continuity

The project delivers an educational platform in Spanish with 16 historical objects, 3 destinations, 14 3D models, a comparative analysis of 133 missions, and an interactive simulator. The data shows that the lifespan of space missions is highly uneven: half of the operational lunar spacecraft ceased functioning after 34 days, while on Mars, 28 out of every 100 missions last more than 8 years. A major limitation is that the simulator's figures are approximations based on historical data (1959–2026) and not exact predictions, as current commercial missions can reduce costs compared to the historical average.

Following the competition, our roadmap includes three stages: in the short term, gathering feedback from teachers and students, optimizing mobile loading, and publishing the English version along with the open repository; in the medium term, expanding the catalog to include Venus, asteroids, and the moons of Jupiter and Saturn, as well as creating classroom guides; and in the long term, conducting workshops in schools in Lima and throughout Peru, incorporating new missions from Artemis and Mars, and exploring augmented reality formats.

Relevance, Validity and Impact

COSMIC TRACE combines creativity, diversity, and educational impact by transforming space statistics into a visual experience created in Spanish by five young people from Lima, Peru. Its validity is supported by official NASA sources, the selection of appropriate statistical measures—such as explaining why the median better describes skewed behavior than the mean—and direct verification of the simulator against real missions like Perseverance, Chandrayaan-3, Hope, Chang'e 7, MMX, ESCAPADE, and Rosalind Franklin.

In conclusion, the objects we leave in space continue to tell our story. By combining open data from NASA, 3D visualization, and interactive simulation, COSMIC TRACE invites new generations to wonder why some spacecraft endure and others don't, and to continue exploring the universe with scientific curiosity.
